apush-leq-0018.comparison: The evidence shows differences in scale, demography, work, and resistance between the regions.
apush-leq-0018.complexity: Both regions built the same system of hereditary, race-based bondage, so the difference was degree, not kind.
apush-leq-0018.context: Tobacco and rice economies, the shift from indentured servants to enslaved labor, and the growth of the Atlantic slave trade.
apush-leq-0018.evidence_chesapeake: Tobacco grown on smaller farms; the 1662 partus law making slavery hereditary; the 1705 code defining enslaved people as real estate; about 40 percent of Virginia's population enslaved by 1740.
apush-leq-0018.evidence_lower_south: Large-scale rice plantations; enslaved people outnumbering free whites; about 70 percent of South Carolina's population enslaved by 1740; the Stono Rebellion of 1739.
apush-leq-0018.thesis: Slavery in the Chesapeake and the Lower South differed substantially in scale and demography — rice plantations on a large scale with enslaved majorities in the Lower South versus tobacco on smaller farms in the Chesapeake — but both regions built the same hereditary, race-based system, so the difference was one of degree rather than kind.

apush-leq-0019.causation: Fear of a united poor plus cheaper enslaved labor drove the shift.
apush-leq-0019.complexity: The shift was already beginning before 1676, and historians debate whether racism caused enslavement or enslavement produced racism.
apush-leq-0019.context: Tobacco's demand for labor, indentured servitude and the headright system, and the growth of the Atlantic slave trade.
apush-leq-0019.evidence_other_causes: Servants growing scarcer and fractious; the Dutch monopoly ending in 1682 and slave prices falling; the 1662 partus law and the 1705 code building hereditary slavery.
apush-leq-0019.evidence_rebellion: The cross-racial alliance of servants, freedmen, and enslaved people; the burning of Jamestown; planters turning to enslaved Africans afterward.
apush-leq-0019.thesis: Bacon's Rebellion was a major cause of the shift from indentured servitude to enslaved African labor in the Chesapeake, but not the only one — it accelerated a shift also driven by servant scarcity and falling slave prices.

apush-saq-0054.a: One reason was fear: Bacon's Rebellion had united servants, freedmen, and enslaved Black people against the governor, so planters wanted a workforce that could never unite across race again.
apush-saq-0054.b: The rebellion showed planters that a mixed workforce of poor whites and Black laborers could unite against them, since servants, freedmen, and enslaved people fought together against Governor Berkeley; planters answered by shifting to enslaved Africans held for life, divided from poor whites by race.
apush-saq-0054.c: Virginia's laws made slavery hereditary and permanent: the 1662 law said a child's status followed the mother, so children of enslaved women were born enslaved, and the 1705 code gathered those laws together, defining enslaved people as property.

apush-saq-0055.a: The petition's purpose was to protest the traffic in enslaved people — the 'traffik of men-body' — stating the Quakers' opposition to slavery.
apush-saq-0055.b: It came from German Quakers at Germantown, Pennsylvania, in 1688, acting on Quaker moral opposition to slavery at a time when slavery and the slave trade were established and growing in the colonies.
apush-saq-0055.c: The petition was set aside by the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting without action, so it shows opposition existed but had little effect; it cannot prove widespread or effective opposition to slavery.

apush-saq-0056.a: The painting shows enslaved African laborers handling and curing tobacco leaves by hand under open-sided sheds.
apush-saq-0056.b: It illustrates that tobacco labor was done by enslaved Black workers by hand — planters relied on enslaved African labor for tobacco work.
apush-saq-0056.c: The painting's place and artist are unknown, and the palm trees suggest it may show a Caribbean plantation rather than the Chesapeake, so it cannot prove Virginia's sheds looked like these.

apush-saq-0057.a: In the South enslaved people were a large share of the population — about 70 percent in South Carolina and 40 percent in Virginia — working in export agriculture, while in the North only about 20 percent of New York's inhabitants were enslaved and they worked as domestic servants, sailors, and artisans' assistants.
apush-saq-0057.b: The northern colonies had no extensive export agriculture, so slavery there never grew as strong as in the South.
apush-saq-0057.c: Slavery was legal in both regions, and enslaved people were held as property without freedom in both the North and the South.

apush-saq-0058.a: The 1705 code declared that enslaved people — 'Negro, mulatto and Indian slaves' — shall be held to be real estate, property held like land.
apush-saq-0058.b: The code gathered decades of Virginia's slave laws into one set of statutes, fixing enslavement for life and hereditary through the mother, and restricting enslaved people's movement, assembly, and legal rights.
apush-saq-0058.c: The code defined enslaved people by race and held them as property for life, making race itself the mark of bondage — a system of racial control, not a law about individual crimes or debts.
